docs.title: Note

docs.title: License
docs.text: All Jarvis-HEP Tools (including Jarvis-HEP and Jarvis-PLOT) are released under the MIT license. The generated output code of Jarvis-HEP can be freely used according to the MIT license, but as they rely on other (PyPI) released libraries also their License has to be taken into account.

docs.title: Why JarvisPLOT supports both
docs.text: Many workflows need standard Cartesian panels and ternary composition views in one project. JarvisPLOT keeps both under one layer/method model so pipelines stay consistent.

docs.title: Rectangular axes (ax)
docs.text:
Typical coordinate form:

coordinates:
  x: {expr: xx}
  y: {expr: yy}
  z: {expr: z0}

Scale and limits are controlled in frame.ax.

docs.title: Ternary axes (axtri)
docs.text:
Ternary layers can use:

  • projected x, y
  • or composition-style inputs (left, right, bottom) depending on method

docs.title: Profiling projection rule
docs.text:
For ternary preprofiling, JarvisPLOT applies rectangular clustering on projected coordinates:

  • x = bottom + 0.5 * right
  • y = right

This keeps preprocessing stable and avoids maintaining separate profiling algorithms for rect and ternary paths.

docs.title: Relation to tripcolor
docs.text: tripcolor now defaults to axes-space triangulation to keep triangle geometry visually stable under log-scale axes.

docs.title: Command
docs.text: jplot <file.yaml> [options]

docs.title: Positional argument
docs.text: • file: input YAML path

docs.title: Options and intent
docs.text:
• -h, --help: print command usage
  • -v, --version: print installed JarvisPLOT version
  • -d, --debug: show detailed runtime logs (useful for pipeline diagnosis)
  • --parse-data: parse dataset structure and write mapped fields back to YAML
  • --out YAML_FILE: write parsed YAML to a new file (with --parse-data)
  • --inplace: overwrite input YAML in place (with --parse-data)
  • --print: disable logo panel (axlogo) in output
  • --rebuild-cache: clear and rebuild workdir/.cache before plotting

docs.title: Typical usage
docs.text:
jplot ./bin/GM95excess.yaml
jplot ./bin/SUSYRun2_EWMSSM.yaml --debug
jplot ./bin/EggBox_Dynesty_06.yaml --rebuild-cache

docs.title: Practical guidance
docs.text:
• Start with plain run.
  • Add --debug only when you need to inspect pipeline decisions.
  • Use --rebuild-cache only when you intentionally want to invalidate cached preprocessing.

docs.title: Why DataSet is separate from Figures
docs.text: DataSet defines raw input once so many figures can reuse it. This avoids repeating file paths and keeps figure sections focused on plotting intent.

docs.title: Supported types
docs.text:
• csv
  • hdf5

docs.title: Common fields
docs.text:
DataSet:
  - name: df
    path: ./data/large.csv
    type: csv

docs.title: HDF5-specific fields
docs.text:
• dataset: select group/root for extraction
  • is_gambit: apply GAMBIT-style validity filtering when relevant
  • columnmap: rename raw columns to stable plotting names

docs.title: Path resolution behavior
docs.text:
• absolute path: unchanged
  • relative path: resolved from project.workdir
  • if project.workdir is absent: resolved from YAML directory

This rule makes moving projects easier: you can relocate the YAML + workdir tree without rewriting every path.

docs.title: Lazy loading behavior
docs.text:
JarvisPLOT registers datasets lazily:

  • it reads lightweight metadata first
  • full table load happens only when a layer pipeline requests the source
  • loaded data is reused through shared context

This is especially useful when one run contains many figures but only some require heavy data.

docs.title: Summary output and summary cache
docs.text: JarvisPLOT prints table summary information and caches it under .cache/summary. If a pipeline later hits cache, summary output can still be emitted for visibility.

docs.title: Q1. Plotting is still slow on very large tables. Why?
docs.text:
Common reasons:

  • cache directory changed or is not reused
  • source fingerprint changed so cache was invalidated
  • pre-profile transforms changed
  • --rebuild-cache was enabled

Start by checking project.workdir/.cache reuse.

docs.title: Q2. I changed profile bin. Should preprofiling rerun?
docs.text:
Default behavior: no.

  • preprofiling is reused
  • runtime profiling reruns with new bin

This is intentional for fast iterative redraws.

docs.title: Q3. I see triangulation warnings with invalid values.
docs.text:
Typical cause is non-finite z (NaN or Inf) in triangulated coloring. JarvisPLOT tripcolor masks triangles touching invalid z, leaving holes.

If needed, add an explicit filter:

- filter: "np.isfinite(z0)"

docs.title: Q4. Relative dataset path is not where I expected.
docs.text:
Resolution rule:

  • relative DataSet.path is based on project.workdir
  • if workdir is missing, YAML directory is used

docs.title: Q5. combine: separate does not work.
docs.text:
Current compatibility keyword is:

  • combine: seperate

docs.title: Q6. How do I force full cache refresh?
docs.text: jplot your.yaml --rebuild-cache

docs.title: Design idea
docs.text:
A Figure describes visual layout and render intent. A Layer describes one data-to-graphic mapping step.

This separation makes complex figures easier to maintain:

  • frame settings stay stable
  • layer pipelines can evolve independently

docs.title: Figure structure
docs.text:
Figures:
  - name: pL2L4_ProfLogL
    enable: true
    style: [a4paper_2x1, rectcmap]
    frame:
      ax: {...}
      axc: {...}
    layers:
      - ...

docs.title: Layer structure
docs.text:
- name: prof
  data:
    - source: df
      transform:
        - profile: {...}
  share_data: pL2L4
  axes: ax
  method: voronoi
  coordinates:
    x: {expr: xx}
    y: {expr: yy}
    z: {expr: z0}
  style:
    cmap: jarvis_rainbow2_r

docs.title: How a layer is processed
docs.text:
1. resolve data.source
  2. apply transform chain in order
  3. evaluate coordinates expressions
  4. call rendering method with merged style
  5. optionally publish result via share_data

docs.title: data.source
docs.text:
Supports:

  • single source name: source: df
  • list source concatenation: source: [df0, df1, df2]

docs.title: share_data
docs.text: If set, layer output is stored under that name and can be reused by later layers. This is helpful when many layers depend on the same expensive preprocessing.

docs.title: combine
docs.text:
Observed modes:

  • default concatenation behavior
  • split behavior with combine: seperate

Note:

  • current keyword is seperate (kept for compatibility with existing YAML files)

docs.title: Axes names
docs.text:
Common axis ids:

  • ax for rectangular plots
  • axtri for ternary plots
  • ax0, ax1, ... for multi-panel layouts

docs.title: Functions and Interpolators
docs.text: Functions lets you define reusable interpolation helpers once and call them in expressions later.

docs.title: Why this exists
docs.text: Without Functions, users often duplicate interpolation code in multiple transforms. Centralizing helpers in YAML improves consistency and avoids copy-paste errors.

docs.title: Current common pattern
docs.text:
• method: interp1d
  • source table from CSV
  • options like kind: linear and bounds: clamp

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Functions:
  - name: FASER2
    source:
      type: csv
      path: ../Workshop/HinoLLP/Fns/FASER2_620.csv
      x: "np.log(y)"
      y: "x"
      sort_by: "y"
      drop_duplicates: "y"
    method: interp1d
    options:
      kind: linear
      bounds: clamp

docs.title: Runtime behavior
docs.text: JarvisPLOT loads these function specs and registers callable helpers into expression evaluation context. After registration, transforms and coordinate expressions can call them directly.

docs.title: JarvisPLOT Documentation
docs.text:
JarvisPLOT is a standalone plotting module built around one idea:

  • you describe plotting intent in YAML
  • the engine handles data loading, transform pipelines, caching, and rendering

This design keeps plotting reproducible and scalable, especially when the same large dataset is reused across many figures.

docs.title: How JarvisPLOT thinks about a run
docs.text:
At runtime, JarvisPLOT treats your YAML in three layers:

  1. DataSet: where raw data comes from and how it should be identified.
  2. Figures/Layers: what each figure should draw and how layers combine.
  3. Transforms/Methods: how data is reduced and which visual primitive is used.

For large tables, JarvisPLOT also applies preprofiling and project-local caching so repeated redraws do not repeatedly scan the full source data.

docs.title: Covered feature set
docs.text:
From the current reference YAML set, common features are:

  • Data types: csv, hdf5
  • Layer methods: voronoi, voronoif, scatter, plot, fill, hist, tripcolor
  • Transforms: add_column, filter, sortby, profile
  • Profile grids: rect, ternary
  • Shared layer data: share_data
  • Optional runtime interpolation helpers: Functions
  • Project-local cache: project.workdir/.cache

docs.title: Plot Methods
docs.text: JarvisPLOT methods map pipeline outputs to concrete visual primitives.

docs.title: Commonly used methods
docs.text:
• voronoi
  • voronoif
  • scatter
  • plot
  • fill
  • hist
  • tripcolor

docs.title: Method selection intuition
docs.text:
• use scatter for raw sample visibility
  • use voronoi/voronoif for profile-like scalar fields over irregular points
  • use tripcolor for triangulated continuous coloring
  • use hist for 1D distributions and weighted counts

docs.title: tripcolor behavior
docs.text:
Current default behavior:

  • triangulation and rendering are in axes space (axes.transAxes)
  • this avoids geometric distortion under mixed axis transforms such as log scale
  • non-finite z values are masked; touching triangles are skipped (holes remain)

To force data-space triangulation:

style:
  space: data

To interpolate color inside triangles:

style:
  shading: gouraud

docs.title: Additional registered method keys
docs.text:
JarvisPLOT also supports Matplotlib-like keys such as:

  • errorbar, bar, barh, step
  • imshow, pcolor, pcolormesh
  • contour, contourf, tricontour, tricontourf, triplot

docs.title: Why two profiling stages exist
docs.text:
Full profiling on very large tables can be expensive when many figures repeat similar work. JarvisPLOT therefore separates the workflow:

  • a fast preprofiling reduction for reuse
  • the full profiling behavior used for final rendering

This preserves interactive iteration speed while keeping final profile logic explicit.

docs.title: Stage 1: Preprofiling (_preprofiling)
docs.text:
• goal: quickly reduce candidates on high-resolution bins (default around 1000 x 1000)
  • output: compact intermediate dataframe for downstream profile/render steps
  • scope: preprocessing only, not a replacement for final profile semantics

docs.title: Stage 2: Runtime profiling (profiling)
docs.text:
• goal: apply the plotting-facing profile behavior
  • effect: this is the stage users tune most when changing visual profile sharpness

docs.title: Cache layout
docs.text:
Under project.workdir:

  • .cache/data/: cached pipeline dataframes
  • .cache/summary/: dataset summary cache
  • .cache/named/: named layer cache (share_data)
  • .cache/manifest.json: fingerprints and metadata

docs.title: What triggers preprofile rebuild
docs.text:
Preprofile cache is invalidated when:

  • source fingerprint changes (size/mtime/md5)
  • transforms before profile change
  • preprofile-relevant options change (coordinates, objective, grid_points, pregrid, pregrid_bin)
  • --rebuild-cache is used

Changing runtime profile bin alone does not force preprofile rebuild by default.

docs.title: Batch prebuild behavior
docs.text:
For multiple figures that share identical input data before profile:

  • JarvisPLOT groups them together
  • builds base dataframe once
  • generates multiple profile masks/results from that one base

This is why repeated map families can scale much better than naive per-figure full scans.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: pip install jarvisplot

docs.title: Run a YAML
docs.text: jplot path/to/config.yaml

docs.title: Rebuild cache (when needed)
docs.text:
jplot path/to/config.yaml --rebuild-cache

Use --rebuild-cache when you want to fully refresh cached preprocessing outputs.

docs.title: Minimal YAML
docs.text:
output:
  dpi: 300
  formats: [png]

project:
  name: Demo
  # workdir is optional

DataSet:
  - name: df
    path: ./data/example.csv
    type: csv

Figures:
  - name: demo_scatter
    enable: true
    style: [a4paper_2x1, rectcmap]
    frame:
      ax:
        labels:
          x: x
          y: y
    layers:
      - name: points
        data:
          - source: df
        axes: ax
        method: scatter
        coordinates:
          x: {expr: x}
          y: {expr: y}
        style:
          s: 2

docs.title: What happens after jplot starts
docs.text:
1. YAML is loaded.
  2. project.workdir and output/cache locations are resolved.
  3. datasets are registered lazily (loaded only when a pipeline needs them).
  4. profile-related prebuild pipelines may be prepared.
  5. layers are rendered and files are saved.

This is why you can keep YAML declarative while still getting optimized behavior for large inputs.

docs.title: Path and output defaults
docs.text:
For DataSet.path:

  • absolute path: used as-is
  • relative path: resolved from project.workdir
  • if project.workdir is omitted: YAML file directory is used

For outputs:

  • if output.dir is omitted, JarvisPLOT uses <workdir>/plots/
  • cache is stored in <workdir>/.cache/

docs.title: Transforms
docs.text: Transforms are the core data pipeline language in JarvisPLOT. They are executed in listed order.

docs.title: Why this design
docs.text: By chaining small transforms, users can iteratively refine data logic without rewriting plotting code. It also allows JarvisPLOT to cache expensive intermediate behavior.

docs.title: Supported transforms
docs.text:
• filter
  • add_column
  • sortby
  • profile

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
transform:
  - add_column:
      name: LogLike_total
      expr: LogL_01 + LogL_02
  - sortby: LogLike_total
  - filter: "X2tot < 10"
  - profile:
      bin: 150
      coordinates:
        x: {expr: Lambda4, scale: linear, name: xx, lim: [-1.5, 1.5]}
        y: {expr: Lambda2, scale: linear, name: yy, lim: [-1.5, 1.5]}
        z: {expr: X2tot, scale: linear, name: z0}
      objective: min
      grid_points: rect

docs.title: filter
docs.text: Use for fast row selection via boolean expressions. JarvisPLOT evaluates expressions in dataframe context.

docs.title: add_column
docs.text: Use for derived features (for example combined likelihood terms). This keeps reusable derived logic in YAML instead of ad-hoc scripts.

docs.title: sortby
docs.text: Use before profile-like reductions when order matters. Commonly paired with objective-based profiling workflows.

docs.title: profile
docs.text:
Main high-level reduction transform for profile-like maps. Key parameters:

  • bin
  • coordinates
  • objective
  • grid_points

In optimized runs, JarvisPLOT may prebuild a preprofiling stage before runtime profiling.

docs.title: YAML Schema
docs.text:
JarvisPLOT YAML is organized so each top-level block answers a different question:

  • DataSet: what data exists
  • Figures: what to draw
  • project/output: where to place work artifacts and outputs
  • Functions (optional): helper interpolators usable in expressions

Typical top-level shape:

output: ...
project: ...
version: ...
DataSet: ...
Functions: ...   # optional
Figures: ...

docs.title: output
docs.text:
output:
  dir: ./Plots            # optional
  dpi: 300
  formats: [png, pdf]

How JarvisPLOT handles it:

  • if dir is relative, it is interpreted from project.workdir
  • if dir is omitted, default becomes <workdir>/plots/

docs.title: project
docs.text:
project:
  name: My Plot Project
  workdir: /path/to/workdir   # optional

How JarvisPLOT handles it:

  • workdir defines where cache and default outputs live
  • if missing, YAML directory is used as workdir

docs.title: DataSet
docs.text:
DataSet:
  - name: df
    path: ./data/file.csv
    type: csv

HDF5 variant:

DataSet:
  - name: h5
    path: ./data/file.hdf5
    type: hdf5
    dataset: data
    is_gambit: true
    columnmap:
      list:
        - source_name: old_col
          new_name: new_col

Design intent:

  • keep source definition explicit
  • allow later layers to reference data by stable logical name (name)

docs.title: Functions (optional)
docs.text:
Functions:
  - name: F1
    source:
      type: csv
      path: ./Fns/f1.csv
      x: "x"
      y: "y"
      sort_by: "x"
    method: interp1d
    options:
      kind: linear
      bounds: clamp

Design intent:

  • predefine reusable helper functions once
  • call them later inside expressions without duplicating logic

docs.title: Figures
docs.text:
Figures:
  - name: FigureName
    enable: true
    style: [a4paper_2x1, rectcmap]
    frame: {...}
    layers: [...]

Design intent:

  • separate visual structure (frame/style) from data flow (layers.data.transform)
  • make each layer independently testable and reusable

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Jarvis-HEP is a pure Python project. No compilation is required, and no system-level dependencies are enforced by default.

In practice, installing Jarvis-HEP only involves:

  1. Downloading the source code

  2. Installing the required Python dependencies

  3. Running it directly

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python ≥ 3.10 (newest Python version prefered)
  • Any Python 3 environment is acceptable, including the system Python, provided that package installation permissions are available. Using an isolated environment (venv, conda, or pyenv) is recommended but not required.

Jarvis-HEP does not rely on any graphical backend and can be safely used on servers, clusters, and other headless environments.

docs.title: Clone the repository from GitHub:
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/pengxuan-zhu-phys/Jarvis-HEP.git
cd Jarvis-HEP

You may also download the source archive manually if preferred.

docs.title: Downloading a Released Version (Recommended)
docs.text:
In addition to cloning the development repository, Jarvis-HEP provides stable released versions.

Released versions are recommended for users who prefer a fixed and well-tested snapshot of the code.

You can download a released source archive from the GitHub Releases page:

  • Navigate to the Releases section of the repository
  • Download the corresponding .zip or .tar.gz source archive
  • Extract it and enter the project directory

This installation guide applies equally to both the development version (cloned from Git) and released source archives.

docs.title: Installing Dependencies
docs.text:
All required Python dependencies are listed in requirements.txt.

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt

It is also recommended to install them inside a virtual environment. Below we show a minimal and reproducible setup using pyenv. Other environment managers can be used equivalently.

docs.title: Using pyenv (optional): example with Python 3.10.12
docs.text:
The version number 3.10.12 is used here as an example. Any newer Python 3.x version compatible with the listed dependencies can be used instead.

pyenv install 3.10.12
pyenv virtualenv 3.10.12 jarvis
pyenv activate jarvis
pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: Running Jarvis-HEP
docs.text:
Jarvis-HEP does not require a formal installation step.

Once the dependencies are installed, it can be executed directly from the source directory:

Jarvis ./bin/EggBox/Example_Bridson.yaml

To run the EggBox example, which is detailed explained in the next page.

Alternatively, Jarvis-HEP can be imported and used as a Python module in custom scripts.

docs.title: External Physics Tools
docs.text:
Jarvis-HEP serves as a workflow and sampling engine.

External physics packages (such as spectrum generators, event generators, or likelihood codes) are not bundled and should be installed separately according to the requirements of each analysis.

Please refer to the corresponding tutorials for concrete examples.

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
• Missing dependencies Ensure all packages listed in requirements.txt are installed in the active Python environment.

  • Multiple Python versions Verify that python and pip refer to the same environment: bash which python which pip

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
After installation, proceed to:

  • Quick Start with Eggbox
  • YAML Format Introduction

docs.title: Tutorial: Declarative Scanning with a 2D Eggbox Example
docs.text:
This tutorial uses Example_Bridson.yaml as a working example.

The point is not the Eggbox model. The point is how to describe a scan in Jarvis-HEP.

If you can follow this example, you can adapt Jarvis-HEP to other problems.

docs.title: The Problem Pattern
docs.text:
To study a Beyond Standard Model numerically, one typically needs to scan its parameter space. Most scan problems look like this:

  • Pick some parameters
  • Explore their values with a sampler
  • Run an external program at each point
  • Save the results

Jarvis-HEP is built for this pattern.

docs.title: Eggbox Function as an Simplifed Package
docs.text:
We begin with the Eggbox function, a purely mathematical function.

The Eggbox function here is defined as a two-dimensional function of two real variables, denoted by x and y.

z(x, y) = (sin(x) * cos(y) + 2)^5

For each input point (x, y), the function returns a single scalar value z. In a realistic physics study, z could represent any theoretical prediction or observable, for example the Higgs boson mass in the MSSM. Without a numerical scan, it is hard to see how such an observable behaves across the parameter space.

As shown in the above figure, a three-dimensional surface plot of z(xx, yy) clearly illustrates this structure. This function has several characteristic features: - It is smooth and continuous - It exhibits a highly structured, multi-peak landscape - Many local maxima and minima appear across the parameter space

These features make the Eggbox function a standard test case for sampling algorithms and scanning workflows.

Suppose an experiment measures this observable as

z = 100 ± 10.

Our task is then to identify which regions in the (x, y) parameter space are compatible with this measurement.

To make this numerical study practical, we implement a small package that computes z for any given (x, y).

docs.title: EggBox package （Code see eggbox）
docs.text:
We now move from the mathematical description to the computational abstraction used by Jarvis-HEP.

In Jarvis-HEP, an input point refers to one complete set of parameter values. For the Eggbox example, one input point is the pair (xx, yy).

The Eggbox calculation is not treated as a direct function call. Instead, it is packaged as a small external program, referred to as a calculator.

The calculator follows a strict input–output contract:

  1. Jarvis-HEP writes the current input point to input.json
  2. Jarvis-HEP executes the calculator program
  3. The calculator reads input.json and computes the Eggbox value
  4. The calculator writes results to output.json
  5. Jarvis-HEP reads output.json and records the requested outputs

In this example, the calculator writes: - z: the value of the Eggbox function - Time: a dummy field used to mimic runtime information

From Jarvis-HEP’s perspective, the calculator is a complete black box. Jarvis-HEP does not inspect the internal code or the mathematical expression.

This example demonstrates the core abstraction used by Jarvis-HEP: any function or model can be used, as long as it can be packaged as a program with well-defined inputs and outputs.

docs.title: How Jarvis-HEP Models the Problem
docs.text:
Jarvis-HEP splits the task into parts:

  • Sampling: which points to try
  • Calculation: what to run at each point
  • Workflow: how everything is connected and executed

You do not write scripts to glue these together. You declare them in YAML.

See: - Guide to YAML

docs.title: Step 1: Name the Scan and Outputs
docs.text:
Open Example_Bridson.yaml.

The Scan section does basic setup: - A scan name - Output paths - Bookkeeping info

This section does not change physics or algorithms.

See: - Scan

docs.title: Step 2: Choose a Sampling Method
docs.text:
The Sampling section answers two questions: - Which sampler is used? - Which variables are sampled?

In this example: - The sampler is Bridson - Two variables are defined - Each variable has bounds

Jarvis-HEP uses this to generate points. Nothing is executed yet.

See: - Sampling

docs.title: Step 3: Set Sampler Controls
docs.text:
Some samplers need extra settings.

In Example_Bridson.yaml these include: - A radius - A limit on attempts

These settings affect how points are proposed. They do not affect calculations.

docs.title: Step 4: Declare the Calculation
docs.text:
The Calculators section describes an external program.

Jarvis-HEP treats it as a black box.

You declare: - How inputs are prepared - How the program is run - Where outputs are read from

Jarvis-HEP handles: - Working directories - Execution order - Parallel runs

No glue scripts are needed.

See: - Calculators

docs.title: Step 5: Connect Inputs and Outputs
docs.text:
Inside Calculators, mappings are defined.

These mappings say: - Which sampled variables go to which inputs - Which files or values are read as outputs

This is the only place where sampling meets calculation.

docs.title: Step 6: Check the Environment
docs.text:
The EnvReqs section lists requirements: - Supported systems - Required tools or libraries

Jarvis-HEP checks these before running.

See: - EnvReqs

docs.title: Step 7: Optional Utilities
docs.text:
The Utils section defines shared helpers.

Examples: - Tables - Interpolations - Reusable data

These helpers do not control sampling or execution.

See: - Utils

docs.title: What Jarvis-HEP Does Automatically
docs.text:
From one YAML file, Jarvis-HEP will: - Build the workflow - Generate sampling points - Run the external program - Collect outputs - Save results in a fixed layout

You do not manage loops or job control.

docs.title: Adapting This to Your Own Problem
docs.text:
To use Jarvis-HEP for a new task:

  1. List the parameters you want to scan
  2. Pick a sampling method
  3. Treat your code as a black box
  4. Declare inputs and outputs in YAML
  5. Run Jarvis-HEP

If your task fits this list, it fits Jarvis-HEP.

docs.title: Practical Introduction to YAML Format
docs.text:
Author: Pengxuan Zhu

This document provides a short, practical introduction to YAML for users who are not familiar with the format. This document assumes no prior knowledge of YAML. It is intended to help you read and write YAML files correctly before using them to configure Jarvis-HEP.

YAML is a human-readable data-serialization format commonly used for configuration files.

docs.title: What Is YAML?
docs.text:
YAML stands for “YAML Ain’t Markup Language”. It is designed to be:

  • Easy to read and write
  • Indentation-based
  • Friendly to version control systems

YAML is often used as an alternative to JSON or XML for configuration purposes.

docs.title: 1. Indentation Matters
docs.text:
YAML uses indentation to represent structure. Spaces define hierarchy.

  • Use spaces, not tabs
  • Be consistent (commonly 2 or 4 spaces)

Correct

parent:
  child:
    key: value

Incorrect

parent:
 child:
    key: value

docs.title: 2. Key–Value Pairs
docs.text:
A basic YAML element is a key–value pair:

key: value

Keys are strings. Values can be strings, numbers, booleans, lists, or mappings.

docs.title: 3. Lists
docs.text:
Lists are written using hyphens (-), equivalent to the List object in Python: 

items:
  - apple
  - orange
  - banana

Lists of mappings are also common, equivalent to the Dict object in Python:

users:
  - name: Alice
    role: admin
  - name: Bob
    role: user

docs.title: 4. Strings and Quoting
docs.text:
Most strings do not require quotes.

name: example
path: /tmp/data

Use quotes when: - The string contains special characters - The value could be misinterpreted

expression: "a > b"
version: "1.0"

docs.title: 5. Numbers and Booleans
docs.text:
YAML automatically interprets numbers and booleans.

count: 10
ratio: 0.5
enabled: true
disabled: false

Avoid quoting numbers unless they must be treated as strings.

docs.title: 6. Comments
docs.text:
Comments start with #.

# This is a comment
key: value  # Inline comment

Comments are ignored by the parser.

docs.title: ❌ Using Tabs
docs.text:
key:
\tchild: value

Tabs are not allowed. Always use spaces.

docs.title: ❌ Inconsistent Indentation
docs.text:
key:
  child1: value
   child2: value

Even a single extra space changes the structure.

docs.title: ❌ Missing Spaces After Colon
docs.text:
key:value

Correct form:

key: value

docs.title: ❌ Ambiguous Values
docs.text:
yes: no
on: off

These may be interpreted as booleans in YAML 1.1. Use explicit values or quotes if unsure.

docs.title: Anchors and Aliases
docs.text:
YAML supports reusable blocks using anchors (&) and aliases (*).

defaults: &defaults
  timeout: 10
  retries: 3

task1:
  <<: *defaults
  name: task_one

This reduces duplication in large configuration files.

docs.title: How to Validate YAML
docs.text:
Before using a YAML file, it is strongly recommended to validate it.

Options include: - Online validators (e.g. yamllint) - Command-line tools - Parsing the file in Python using yaml.safe_load

docs.title: Recommended References
docs.text:
• YAML Official Specification

  • YAML Tutorial (Learn X in Y Minutes)

  • PyYAML Documentation

These resources provide deeper explanations and advanced usage examples.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• YAML is indentation-based and human-readable
  • Consistent spacing is critical
  • Start simple and validate often
  • When in doubt, prefer clarity over brevity

Now, you can proceed to the Jarvis-HEP tutorial.
